the father's promise to waive the debt. This is 'illusory' or 'insufficient' consideration.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Consideration must be 'real' and have some value in the eyes of the law.
2. A promise to refrain from an act that one has no legal right to do is not consideration.
3. Vague promises of behavior are not sufficient consideration.

cases.title: Dutton v. Poole
cases.facts:
A father intended to cut down some trees on his land to raise a portion for his daughter's marriage. The son (the
heir) promised the father that if he didn't cut the trees, the son would pay the daughter £1,000. The father died,
and the son refused to pay. The daughter sued.
cases.issues:
1. Can a child sue on a promise made to their parent for their benefit (Privity exception)?
2. Is 'natural love and affection' sufficient to overcome lack of privity?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The daughter argued that she was the intended beneficiary and the consideration (saving the trees) moved from
her father for her sake.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The son argued the classic rule: the daughter was not a party to the contract and provided no consideration.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the daughter.
cases.reasoning:
In this ancient case, the court allowed an exception to the privity rule based on 'blood relationship'. It held that
the father's consideration (not cutting trees) was essentially the same as the daughter's interest. This was a
precursor to the modern 'beneficiary' exceptions. (Note: While later overturned in English law by Tweddle v.
Atkinson, it remains an important historical marker for the Indian position in Chinnaya v. Ramaya).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Early recognition of 'third-party beneficiaries' in close family relations.
2. The concept that consideration can move from a third party (now law in India).
3. Equity often intervenes to prevent family members from profiting through breached promises.

cases.title: Tweddle v. Atkinson
cases.facts:
Following a marriage, the fathers of the couple agreed to each pay the groom a sum. The groom sued for the
money after one father died. This case directly addressed whether the 'relationship' exception in Dutton v.
Poole was still good law.
cases.issues:
1. Does the 'Doctrine of Privity' admit an exception for close family members in English law?
2. Can a beneficiary sue without provided consideration?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The groom relied on Dutton v. Poole, arguing that the relationship between father and child created an
exception.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The defendant argued that only parties who provided consideration could sue.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled against the groom.
cases.reasoning:
The Court definitively established the 'Privity of Contract' and 'Privity of Consideration' as absolute rules in
England. It held that the groom was a 'stranger' to the agreement and the consideration. The Court rejected the
'blood relationship' exception, stating that only the parties who made the exchange could enforce the bond.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Refutation of the family-benefit exception to privity in English law.
2. Consideration must move from the promisee.
3. Strangers to a contract cannot sue even if the contract was made for their specific benefit.

cases.title: Smith v. Hughes
cases.facts:
A farmer (Hughes) sold oats to a racehorse owner (Smith). Smith wanted 'old' oats for his horses. Hughes
showed Smith a sample. Smith examined it and bought the whole batch. When the oats were delivered, they
were 'new' oats. Smith refused to pay. Hughes sued, arguing that he never promised they were 'old'-he just
showed the sample.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Mistake' regarding a quality of an item void a contract?
2. What is the rule of 'Caveat Emptor' (Buyer Beware) in contracts?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The buyer (Smith) argued that the seller knew he only bought old oats. Selling new oats was a breach based on
a fundamental mistake of the subject matter.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The seller (Hughes) argued he made no misrepresentation. Smith looked at the sample and formed his own
conclusion. Silence about a quality is not a lie.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the seller, Hughes.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that unless there is a 'warranty' or a 'fraud', a mistake as to the quality of the goods does not
void the contract. Hughes was silent, and silence is not fraud. Smith had the chance to inspect the sample. If he
made a wrong inference, he must suffer the loss. The contract was for the 'specific oats' shown, and the price
was agreed. Mistake as to quality is not a 'mistake as to substance'.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Caveat Emptor: The buyer must look after their own interests.
2. Mistake of quality (unless induced by fraud) does not void a contract.
3. Subjective intent is irrelevant if the objective conduct shows agreement on the item.

cases.title: Cundy v. Lindsay
cases.facts:
A rogue named Blenkarn ordered linen from Lindsay. He signed the order such that it looked like it was from
'Blenkiron & Co.', a reputable firm in the same street. Lindsay, thinking they were dealing with the reputable
firm, sent the goods. Blenkarn didn't pay and sold the goods to Cundy. Lindsay sued Cundy for the return of the
goods.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Mistake as to Identity' make a contract void or voidable?
2. Can a third party get good title from a person who committed 'identity fraud'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Lindsay argued they never intended to sell to Blenkarn. They intended to sell to Blenkiron & Co. Therefore,
there was no contract at all, and the title never left them.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Cundy argued they were innocent buyers. The contract was at most 'voidable' for fraud, and since Lindsay
didn't cancel it before Cundy bought, Cundy got good title.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of Lindsay.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that where a party intends to deal with a 'specific' person and deals with someone else by
mistake, the contract is 'V oid' (not just voidable). Since Lindsay only intended to contract with Blenkiron &
Co., there was never a 'meeting of minds' with the rogue. Because the contract was void, the rogue never got
the 'title' to the goods and could not pass it to Cundy. Lindsay could take their goods back from the innocent
buyer.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Mistake as to identity of the person renders a contract void ab initio.
2. No title passes under a void contract.
3. Distinguished from 'Mistake of Attribute' where the contract is only voidable.

cases.title: Phillips v. Brooks Ltd
cases.facts:
A rogue entered a jewelry shop and selected a ring. He claimed to be 'Sir George Bullough' and gave a fake
address. The jeweler checked the directory, saw Sir George existed at that address, and allowed the rogue to
pay by cheque and take the ring. The cheque bounced. The rogue sold the ring to Brooks (a pawnbroker). The
jeweler sued Brooks.
cases.issues:
1. What is the difference between identity fraud 'by post' and 'face-to-face'?
2. Does a face-to-face deal with a rogue create a void or voidable contract?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The jeweler argued Cundy v. Lindsay: he only intended to sell to Sir George. Therefore, the contract was
void and no title passed.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The pawnbroker argued that the jeweler intended to sell to the person standing in front of him. The identity was
just an 'attribute' (creditworthiness). The contract was voidable for fraud, but valid until cancelled.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the pawnbroker.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the 'Face-to-Face' rule. When parties are physically present, there is a strong presumption
that the seller intends to contract with the person in front of them, regardless of what name they use. The
'identity' was a mistake, but the 'individual' was certain. Therefore, the contract was only 'voidable' for fraud.
Since the jeweler didn't cancel the contract before the rogue sold the ring, the innocent buyer (Brooks) got a
valid title.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Face-to-face identity fraud generally makes a contract voidable, not void.
2. The seller is presumed to contract with the person physically present.
3. Title passes to innocent third parties under voidable contracts before rescission.

cases.title: Ingram v. Little
cases.facts:
Three ladies sold a car to a rogue who claimed to be a respectable businessman. They were suspicious and
refused his cheque. The rogue then gave them a name and address. The ladies went to a nearby post office,
checked the phone book, and confirmed the person existed. Only then did they accept the cheque. The cheque
bounced and the rogue sold the car to Little.
cases.issues:
1. Can a face-to-face contract be void for identity mistake if the seller takes extraordinary steps to verify
the person?
2. Does verification override the 'face-to-face' presumption?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The ladies argued that they made it clear they would not sell to him as a person. They only agreed to sell
because they believed he was the person in the phone book. Identity was paramount.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Little argued the standard Phillips v. Brooks rule: they sold to the man in front of them.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the ladies, holding the contract void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the ladies had rebutted the 'face-to-face' presumption. By checking the phone book and
refusing the cheque until the identity was 'confirmed', they showed that the identity of the buyer was the sole
reason for the contract. Since the buyer was not that person, there was no contract. (Note: This case is often
criticized as being inconsistent with other identity cases).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Presumptions in face-to-face deals can be rebutted by evidence of extreme caution regarding identity.
2. If identity is proven to be 'fundamental' to the deal, the contract is void.
3. This case represents the 'narrow' exception to the Phillips v. Brooks rule.

cases.title: Raffles v. Wichelhaus
cases.facts:
The defendant agreed to buy a cargo of cotton from the plaintiff to arrive from Bombay on a ship named
'Peerless'. Unknown to both parties, there were two ships named 'Peerless' leaving Bombay: one in October and
one in December. The buyer meant the October ship; the seller meant the December ship. When the cotton
arrived on the December ship, the buyer refused to take it.
cases.issues:
1. What happens if there is a 'Mutual Mistake' regarding the subject matter?
2. Is a contract valid if there is an 'ambiguity' that prevents a meeting of minds?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The seller argued the contract was for 'cotton on the Peerless'. The cotton arrived on a ship called Peerless, so
the buyer must pay.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer argued that the timing was everything. Since they were talking about different ships, they were
talking about different contracts.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the buyer.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that since both ships fit the description perfectly, the ambiguity was 'latent'. There was no
consensus ad idem (meeting of minds) because the parties were referring to different ships. Since the contract
was incapable of a single certain meaning, no binding agreement ever existed. Both parties were under a
genuine mutual mistake.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Mutual mistake as to the identity of the subject matter makes the contract void (Section 20 ICA).
2. Latent ambiguity prevents the formation of a contract.
3. Subjective intent matters if the objective description is ambiguous.

cases.title: Bell v. Lever Brothers Ltd
cases.facts:
Lever Brothers fired two senior executives and gave them a massive 'Golden Handshake' (compensation) to
leave. Later, the company discovered that the executives had secretly committed breaches of their duties which
would have allowed the company to fire them without paying any compensation. The company sued to get the
money back, claiming the compensation agreement was void for 'Common Mistake'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Common Mistake' regarding a background fact (which makes the contract unnecessary) void
a contract?
2. What is the 'High Threshold' for mistake in property/commercial law?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The company argued both parties believed the executives' employment could not be terminated without pay.
This mistake was fundamental to the payout.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The executives argued that the contract was to end the relationship. The fact that the company could have
ended it differently is a mistake of 'value' or 'motive', not substance.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The House of Lords ruled in favor of the executives.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established that Common Mistake only voids a contract if the mistake is as to the 'existence' of the
subject matter or a quality that makes the contract 'radically different' from what was intended. The 'subject
matter' was the termination of the contracts. That was achieved. The mistake about the necessity of the
payout was not fundamental enough. The law favors the finality of settlements. A mistake as to quality or
background motive is insufficient.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Common mistake must be 'fundamental' and 'radical' to void a contract.
2. Mistakes of 'quality' or 'commercial necessity' are generally not enough.
3. Narrow interpretation of the doctrine of mistake to protect commercial certainty.

cases.title: Foster v. Mackinnon
cases.facts:
An elderly gentleman with poor eyesight was asked to sign a document. He was told it was a mere 'guarantee'
of a minor nature. In reality, it was a 'Bill of Exchange' for a large sum. The bill was later sold to Foster. When
Mackinnon was sued, he claimed the document was not his act (Non est factum).
cases.issues:
1. Can a person be excused from a contract if they were totally mistaken about the 'nature' of the
document they signed?
2. What is the doctrine of 'Non est factum'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The plaintiff argued the signature was genuine. The signer's negligence in not reading it shouldn't affect a third
party.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The signer argued that he never intended to sign a bill of exchange. His mind did not follow his pen. Therefore,
the deed was void.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the defendant, Mackinnon.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that if a person is induced by fraud to sign a document which is 'fundamentally different' in
character from what he thought it was, the signature is a nullity. This applies particularly to the blind, illiterate,
or elderly. Since Mackinnon thought he was signing a guarantee (a promise) but signed a bill of exchange (a
negotiable debt), the mistake was as to the 'class' of the document. The document was 'not his deed'.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Non est factum: A signature is void if the signer is mistaken as to the fundamental nature of the
document.
2. Mistake of 'Character' (nature) vs. Mistake of 'Content' (terms).
3. Requires absence of negligence on the part of the signer.

cases.title: Merritt v. Merritt
cases.facts:
A husband left his wife for another woman. He signed an agreement promising to pay his wife £40 a month and
transfer the house to her if she paid off the remaining mortgage. She paid the mortgage, but he refused to
transfer the house, claiming it was a domestic agreement with no legal intent (relying on Balfour v. Balfour).
cases.issues:
1. Does the presumption against legal intent in domestic agreements apply when the couple has
'separated'?
2. When do spouses intend to create legal relations?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The wife argued that the agreement was made in writing after he left the house. They were not living in amity;
they were negotiating a settlement.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The husband argued Balfour v. Balfour: arrangements between husband and wife are not contracts.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the wife.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the presumption in Balfour v. Balfour only applies when the spouses are living together
in harmony. When a couple is 'separated' or about to separate, they do not rely on 'love and affection'; they
bargain at arm's length to settle their affairs. In such cases, there is a strong presumption that they do intend
their agreements to be legally binding.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Separated spouses are presumed to intend to create legal relations.
2. Context determines the presumption of legal intent.
3. Written settlements between family members in conflict are generally binding contracts.

cases.title: Brogden v. Metropolitan Railway Co.
cases.facts:
This case (revisited for performance aspects) dealt with whether supplier Brogden could be bound to a price
draft he never formally signed, but which both parties followed for months.
cases.issues:
1. Can the 'last shot' (the final version of a document) become the contract through performance?
2. Does 'silence' combined with 'action' constitute acceptance?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The railway argued that by acting on the price, Brogden accepted the terms.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Brogden argued he was just doing his job and there was no new contract.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court held a contract existed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court ruled that while 'silence' alone is not acceptance, 'silence' followed by the active performance of the
specific terms is the strongest possible acceptance. By delivering coal at the new price, Brogden manifested his
consent.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Course of conduct is a valid mode of acceptance.
2. Executed consideration (doing the act) creates a binding bond.
3. Commercial consistency is protected by the law.

cases.title: Central Inland Water Transport Corp v. Brojo Nath Ganguly
cases.facts:
A government corporation's employment rules contained a clause: 'The services of a permanent employee can
be terminated by the management at any time by giving 3 months' notice without giving any reason'. A senior
manager was fired using this clause. He challenged it as 'unconscionable' and against public policy.
cases.issues:
1. Can the Court strike down an 'Unconscionable' clause in a commercial or employment contract?
2. Does 'Inequality of Bargaining Power' make a contract void under Section 23 of the ICA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The employee argued that he had no choice but to sign. The rule was 'take it or leave it'. It gave the employer
dictatorial powers, which is against public policy.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The Corporation argued 'freedom of contract'. The employee was highly educated and joined voluntarily.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court struck down the clause as void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that in cases of 'gross inequality of bargaining power', the principle of freedom of contract is a
myth. Where one party (the State or a large employer) dictates terms to a weaker party who has no choice but
to accept, the court will strike down terms that are 'unreasonable, unfair, and unconscionable'. The 'hire and fire'
rule was found to be 'oppressive' and against the public policy of India (Section 23). This established the
'Doctrine of Unconscionability' in Indian contract law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Unconscionable contracts are void under Section 23 ICA as being against public policy.
2. Courts will protect the weaker party in cases of 'take-it-or-leave-it' (Adhesion) contracts.
3. Public Sector employers must act fairly and reasonably.

cases.title: Kundan Lal v. State of U.P.
cases.facts:
A government official threatened a contractor that his existing contracts would be cancelled and his security
deposit forfeited unless he agreed to sign a new contract at a much lower rate. Fearing financial ruin, the
contractor signed the new agreement. Later, he sued to set aside the contract, claiming it was obtained through
'coercion'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a threat to cause economic loss or cancel existing legal rights constitute 'Coercion' under Section
15 of the ICA?
2. What is the scope of 'Economic Duress' in Indian Law?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The contractor argued that his consent was not free. The threat of financial ruin was an unlawful pressure that
forced him to sign an unfavorable deal.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The State argued that they were merely exercising their administrative discretion. There was no 'criminal' act or
threat to life/limb, so Section 15 was not triggered.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the contractor, setting aside the agreement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that although Section 15 of the ICA defines coercion as the 'committing or threatening to
commit any act forbidden by the IPC', Indian courts also recognize the broader doctrine of 'Economic Duress'.
Where one party has no choice but to submit to the demands of a powerful party to save their business or
property, the consent is vitiated. The threat to illegally cancel contracts and seize deposits was an unlawful
exercise of power designed to obtain an unfair advantage, making the contract voidable.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Consent obtained through economic duress is voidable.
2. Pressure that leaves a party with no 'reasonable alternative' vitiates free consent.
3. Inequality of bargaining power is a factor in determining coercion.

cases.title: Chikham Ammiraju v. Chikham Seshamma
cases.facts:
A Hindu man threatened to commit suicide unless his wife and son executed a release deed in favor of his
brother regarding certain family properties. Fearing for his life, the wife and son signed the deed. Later, they
sued to set aside the deed, claiming it was obtained by 'Coercion'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a threat to commit suicide constitute 'Coercion' under Section 15 of the ICA?
2. Is suicide an act 'forbidden by the Indian Penal Code'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The wife argued that the threat to kill himself was the ultimate form of psychological pressure, forcing her to
sign away her rights against her will.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The brother argued that Section 15 requires a threat to commit an act 'forbidden by the IPC'. While 'attempt' to
suicide is a crime, 'committing' suicide is not (as the person is dead). Therefore, the threat didn't fit the literal
definition.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The High Court ruled in favor of the wife, holding the deed was voidable.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the IPC forbids the attempt to commit suicide. Logically, the threat to commit suicide
includes the threat to 'attempt' it. Therefore, a threat to commit suicide is a threat to do an act forbidden by the
IPC. It is a highly effective form of coercion. Since the wife's consent was obtained through this unlawful
threat, the release deed was voidable at her option under Section 19.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Threat of suicide constitutes 'Coercion' under Section 15 ICA.
2. Consent is not free if obtained through self-harm threats.
3. Section 15 is interpreted to include acts that are criminally punishable or forbidden in principle.

cases.title: Ranganayakamma v. Alwar Setti
cases.facts:
A young widow was forced to adopt a boy and sign a property settlement by her relatives. They refused to
allow her to remove the dead body of her husband for cremation until she signed the documents. She signed,
and later sued to set them aside.
cases.issues:
1. Does the 'unlawful detaining of property' under Section 15 include the detention of a dead body?
2. Can the obstruction of a religious/civil duty constitute coercion?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The widow argued that the dead body was her 'property' or at least a sacred charge. Using it as a hostage to
force a contract was a gross and illegal pressure.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The relatives argued that a dead body is not 'property' in the commercial sense defined by the TPA or ICA, so
Section 15 did not apply.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the widow, setting aside the adoption and settlement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the relatives' act of preventing the funeral was a 'wrongful act' designed to compel the
widow's consent. Section 15 defines coercion to include the 'unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any
property'. The Court gave a broad meaning to 'property' and 'detention' to include any act that unlawfully
restricts a person's rights or duties to force a contract. Obstructing the cremation of a loved one is a form of
illegal detention that destroys free consent.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Unlawful pressure via the detention of a body or sacred object is Coercion.
2. Consent must be given in an atmosphere of freedom.
3. Section 15 is designed to prevent the exploitation of emotional or religious vulnerabilities.

cases.title: Mannu Singh v. Umadat Pande
cases.facts:
An elderly devotee, Mannu Singh, executed a gift deed of his entire property in favor of his 'Guru' (spiritual
advisor), Umadat Pande. He did this after the Guru told him that gifting the property would secure 'spiritual
benefit' for the devotee in the afterlife. Later, Mannu Singh sued to cancel the gift, claiming 'Undue Influence'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a spiritual or religious relationship create a presumption of 'Undue Influence' under Section 16
of the ICA?
2. On whom does the burden of proof lie when a gift is made to a person in a fiduciary position?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The devotee argued that as his Guru, Pande was in a position to dominate his mind. The promise of 'spiritual
salvation' was an unfair advantage used to strip him of his worldly goods.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The Guru argued that the gift was voluntary and motivated by the devotee's own religious faith. There was no
'domination', only spiritual guidance.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the devotee, setting aside the gift.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that a 'Guru-Chela' (spiritual) relationship is one of the highest forms of trust and confidence.
Under Section 16(2), a person is deemed to be in a position to dominate the will of another where he stands in a
'fiduciary' relation. In such cases, the law presumes the existence of undue influence if the transaction appears
'unconscionable' (like gifting everything). The burden of proof shifted to the Guru to prove the gift was free and
independent. Since the Guru failed to prove this, the gift was voidable.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Spiritual advisors stand in a fiduciary relationship, giving rise to a presumption of undue influence
(Section 16 ICA).
2. Gifting away one's entire livelihood is an 'unconscionable' act requiring strict proof of voluntariness.
3. The law protects the vulnerable from 'pious' fraud.

cases.title: Takri Devi v. Rama Dogra
cases.facts:
Takri Devi, an illiterate and old woman, signed a document she believed was a 'Lease' allowing someone to
farm her land. In reality, the document was a 'Sale Deed' transferring the ownership. The purchaser paid a price
far below the market rate. She sued to cancel the deed.
cases.issues:
1. What is the scope of 'Undue Influence' in transactions with illiterate or elderly persons?
2. Can 'unconscionable price' trigger a presumption of fraud?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The woman argued that she was deceived. Her illiteracy made her dependent on the purchaser's explanation of
the document. The tiny price proved she didn't understand she was 'selling' the land.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The purchaser argued that she signed in front of a registrar and the contract was sacred. Illiteracy is not a
ground to cancel a registered deed.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of Takri Devi.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that in a transaction between an educated, powerful person and an illiterate, vulnerable person,
the 'Unconscionableness' of the deal (the low price) combined with the 'dominating position' of the purchaser
creates a presumption of undue influence under Section 16(3). The purchaser failed to prove that the
transaction was 'fair, just, and reasonable'. The Court treated the illiterate woman similar to a 'Pardanashin' lady,
requiring the highest standard of protection and clarity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Illiteracy and age are factors creating a 'position of domination' (Section 16).
2. If a transaction appears unconscionable on its face, the burden of proof is on the dominant party.
3. Fairness of price is evidence of free consent.

cases.title: Mercantile Bank of India v. Central Bank of India
cases.facts:
A merchant pledged 'Railway Receipts' (RR) for a cargo of groundnuts to Central Bank to get a loan. Central
Bank later gave the RRs back to the merchant for the 'limited purpose' of clearing the goods. Instead, the rogue
merchant used those same RRs to pledge the goods again to Mercantile Bank and got a second loan. Mercantile
Bank argued they had the superior right because Central Bank's 'negligence' allowed the fraud.
cases.issues:
1. Can a prior pledgee's right be defeated by the 'Estoppel by Negligence' if they return documents to the
pledgor?
2. Who has the priority in 'double pledge' scenarios?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Mercantile Bank argued that by giving the receipts back, Central Bank allowed the merchant to 'appear' as the
owner. They were 'estopped' from claiming their prior right.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Central Bank argued that they were only following standard business practice. Returning documents for
clearing isn't 'negligence'. The first pledge remains a valid 'right in rem'.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Privy Council ruled in favor of Central Bank (the first pledgee).
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that for 'estoppel' to apply, there must be a 'duty of care' owed by the first bank to the second
bank, and a clear breach of it. Central Bank followed a normal trade practice. They did not 'represent' to
Mercantile Bank that the merchant was the owner. The merchant's fraud was an independent act. Since the first
pledge was never legally terminated, it took priority. The second bank took the receipts at their own risk.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Estoppel by Negligence requires a breach of a specific duty.
2. Prior legal interests (pledges) are not easily defeated by subsequent innocent parties.
3. Standard commercial practices are not considered 'negligence' in property/contract law.

cases.title: Shive Sahai v. Inayat Singh
cases.facts:
A borrower was in urgent need of money to pay a fine to stay out of jail. The lender agreed to the loan only if
the borrower agreed to an exorbitant interest rate (75% per annum) and a clause allowing the lender to seize all
the borrower's lands on a single default. The borrower sued to reduce the interest rate.
cases.issues:
1. Does 'Urgent Need' of the borrower allow the lender to dominate his will?
2. Can an 'unconscionable interest rate' be struck down as being obtained through undue influence?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The borrower argued that the lender took advantage of his desperate situation (fear of jail). The terms were so
harsh that no sane person would agree to them unless forced.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued 'freedom of contract'. The borrower was a competent adult. High risk justifies high interest.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the borrower, reducing the interest rate.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that while 'urgent need' alone is not undue influence, if a lender uses that need to extract
'unconscionable' terms, Section 16 is triggered. The 75% rate was 'shocks the conscience' of the court. The
Court ruled that the lender was in a position to dominate the will of the desperate borrower and used that
position to gain an 'unfair advantage'. The Court used its equitable power to 're-open' the contract and fix a fair
interest rate.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Unconscionable interest rates are evidence of undue influence.
2. Exploitation of 'urgent need' vitiates free consent.
3. Courts can modify 'unfair' terms in money-lending contracts.

cases.title: Couturier v. Hastie
cases.facts:
A seller sold a cargo of corn that was supposed to be in transit from Greece to England. Unknown to both the
seller and the buyer, the corn had fermented during the voyage and had already been sold by the ship's captain
at an intermediate port before the contract was signed. The buyer refused to pay.
cases.issues:
1. Is a contract valid if the subject matter has already ceased to exist at the time of the agreement?
2. What is the effect of 'Mutual Mistake as to Existence' (Section 20 ICA)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The seller argued that the buyer bought the 'risk' of the voyage. The buyer should pay the price and claim from
insurance.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer argued that the contract was for the 'sale of goods'. Since there were no goods to sell at the time of
the deal, there was no contract.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the buyer.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the foundation of the contract was the existence of the specific cargo of corn. Since the
corn did not exist as 'commercial corn' at the moment of the sale, there was a fundamental 'mutual mistake' that
went to the heart of the deal. Therefore, the contract was void from the beginning. You cannot buy or sell
something that isn't there.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Mutual mistake regarding the 'existence' of the subject matter makes a contract void (Section 20 ICA).
2. No liability arises under a void agreement.
3. The 'risk' only passes if the goods actually exist at the time of the contract.

cases.title: Boulton v. Jones
cases.facts:
Jones used to deal with a shopkeeper named Brocklehurst. He sent an order for goods to Brocklehurst.
However, on that very day, Brocklehurst had sold his business to Boulton. Boulton supplied the goods without
telling Jones about the change in ownership. Jones consumed the goods and then refused to pay Boulton,
claiming he only wanted to deal with Brocklehurst (to whom he owed money and wanted to set off the debt).
cases.issues:
1. Can an offer be accepted by a person to whom it was NOT made?
2. Does a mistake of 'Identity' prevent the formation of a contract?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Boulton argued that Jones got the goods he wanted at the right price. Who supplied them is irrelevant. Jones
should pay for what he consumed.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Jones argued that he had a specific reason to deal with Brocklehurst (the set-off). He never made an offer to
Boulton, so there was no contract with him.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of Jones.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'where a contract is made with a specific person, no other person can step in and accept the
offer'. Jones had a right to choose his contracting party. Since Boulton knew the offer was meant for
Brocklehurst and concealed the truth, there was no 'meeting of minds'. Jones was not liable to pay Boulton.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. An offer can only be accepted by the person to whom it is addressed.
2. Identity of the party is fundamental if there is a specific motive for the choice.
3. One cannot be forced into a contract with a stranger.

cases.title: L'Estrange v Graucob
cases.facts:
A woman signed an order form for an automatic cigarette machine. The form had a small clause excluding all
implied warranties. The machine didn't work. She sued, claiming she hadn't read the small print.
cases.issues:
1. Is the signer bound if they don't read the terms?
2. Does the lack of 'reasonable notice' apply to signed documents?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The woman argued that the clause was tiny and she wasn't given 'notice' of its harsh nature, relying on the
'ticket cases'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The seller argued that a signature is different from a ticket; it's a formal declaration of consent to all terms.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the seller.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'reasonable notice' rule only applies to unsigned documents (like tickets or wall signs).
When a person signs a document, they are bound by its contents in the absence of fraud. The signature is an
absolute barrier that prevents the party from claiming ignorance.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Signature rule is absolute in the absence of fraud.
2. No 'notice' requirement for terms in a signed contract.
3. Parties are responsible for what they sign.

cases.title: Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya
cases.facts:
Two partners entered into an agreement to carry on 'wagering' (gambling) transactions on the price of wheat.
While wagering itself was not illegal under criminal law, Section 30 of the ICA makes wagering agreements
'void'. One partner suffered a loss and the other partner sued him to recover his share of the loss under their
partnership contract.
cases.issues:
1. Is a partnership or a collateral agreement to a 'void' contract also void?
2. What is the distinction between 'void' and 'illegal' under Section 23 of the ICA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The defendant argued that since the main business (wagering) was void, the partnership to do that business was
'opposed to public policy' and thus illegal under Section 23.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The plaintiff argued that wagering is only 'void' (unenforceable), not 'forbidden by law' (illegal). Therefore, a
secondary contract to share the results of a void act is still valid.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, allowing the recovery.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on 'Public Policy'. It held that judges should not invent new heads of
public policy. Wagering is merely 'void' under Section 30. It is not 'illegal' or 'immoral' in the eyes of the law. A
'void' contract is like a blank space, but an 'illegal' contract is a 'forbidden' space. Since the partnership was a
collateral agreement and the underlying act wasn't 'forbidden', the partner could recover the money. This
established that 'void' acts don't necessarily taint secondary contracts.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 23 ICA: 'Public Policy' is a narrow doctrine.
2. Agreements collateral to a 'void' contract (like wagering) are enforceable.
3. Difference between 'void' (not enforceable) and 'illegal' (prohibited).

cases.title: Hadley v Baxendale
cases.facts:
This case (revisited) established the rules for 'general' damages. The carrier failed to deliver a mill shaft,
causing the mill to stay closed.
cases.issues: 1. What are 'Natural' damages?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued the carrier should pay for all the days the mill didn't work.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The carrier argued he only agreed to 'deliver a shaft', not to 'run a mill'.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled for the carrier.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that damages must arise 'naturally in the usual course of things'. In 1854, a carrier wouldn't
naturally assume that a mill only had one shaft. Most mills had spares. Therefore, the total shutdown was an
unusual (special) circumstance. Since the carrier wasn't told about the lack of a spare, he wasn't liable for the
shutdown, only for the cost of the delay itself.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. First Limb: Damages must be natural and probable.
2. General damages require no special notice.
3. Objective foreseeability is the test for liability.

cases.title: Philips v Brooks
cases.facts:
A rogue in a shop claimed to be 'Sir George Bullough' and paid for a ring with a bad cheque. The jeweler let
him take it after checking the directory.
cases.issues: 1. Was the mistake about 'Identity' or 'Attribute'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The jeweler argued he only intended to sell to the 'Real' Sir George. Thus, no contract with the rogue.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer argued the jeweler intended to sell to the 'man in the shop'. His name was just a reason to trust his
credit (an attribute).
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled it was a 'Mistake of Attribute'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that in face-to-face deals, you are presumed to contract with the physical person. The mistake
about his name and wealth was a mistake about his 'qualities' (attributes), not his 'identity' as a human being. A
contract vitiated by attribute-fraud is 'voidable' (valid until cancelled). Since it wasn't cancelled in time, the
rogue could pass a good title to a third party.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Mistake of Attribute: Makes a contract voidable for fraud.
2. Mistake of Identity: Makes a contract void ab initio.
3. Face-to-face transactions favor the 'voidable' interpretation.

cases.title: Auckland Corp v. Elias
cases.facts:
A city council agreed to lease land to a person with a clause: 'The rent shall be a fair and reasonable amount to
be agreed upon by the parties'. Later, they couldn't agree on the amount, and the council claimed the lease was
void for uncertainty.
cases.issues:
1. Does 'Agreement to Agree' create a binding contract?
2. Can the court fix a 'reasonable price' under Section 29?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The tenant argued that 'fair and reasonable' is a clear standard that a court or valuer can determine. The intent
was to have a lease.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The council argued that since the parties themselves had to agree and hadn't, there was no consensus on the
most vital term: the rent.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled the lease was void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that an 'agreement to agree' on a fundamental term like price or rent is too uncertain to be a
contract. Under Section 29, the terms must be 'certain' or 'capable of being made certain'. If the certainty
depends on the 'future whim' of the parties, the court will not step in to perform their negotiations for them. The
agreement was a nullity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Agreement to agree is not a contract.
2. Fundamental terms (price/rent) must be fixed or have a clear formula for calculation.
3. The court will not rewrite a contract to make it certain.

cases.title: Balfour v Balfour
cases.facts: This case (revisited) established the 'Presumption' against legal intent in families.
cases.issues: 1. Is the presumption 'rebuttable'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The wife argued the promise was a solemn financial arrangement for her survival.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The husband argued it was just 'husband-wife talk'.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled for the husband.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the law of contract is 'not for the breakfast table'. In domestic settings, there is a strong
starting presumption that no legal bond is intended. This can only be overcome by clear evidence, such as a
formal written document or where the parties are already in a state of conflict (like Merritt v. Merritt).
Without such evidence, the promise remains a moral one only.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Presumption of lack of legal intent in social/domestic cases.
2. Policy reason: To prevent the 'floodgates' of litigation between relatives.
3. Objectivity is the key to determining intent.

cases.title: Derry v Peek
cases.facts:
This case (revisited) defined the boundary between 'Carelessness' and 'Fraud'. Directors thought they had a
tram license; they didn't.
cases.issues: 1. Is 'negligence' the same as 'fraud'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Plaintiffs argued the directors had 'no business' stating it as a fact without checking.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Defendants argued they 'honestly believed' it was a certainty.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled it was not fraud.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'fraud' is a serious allegation. It requires a 'wicked mind'. If a person is simply stupid,
optimistic, or careless, but honestly thinks they are telling the truth, they are not a 'fraudster'. For fraud, you
must prove the person 'knew it was a lie' or was 'reckless' to the point of not caring about the truth at all.
Negligence is a separate legal field.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Fraud requires a 'guilty mind' (Mens Rea).
2. Honest belief is a complete defense to a charge of fraud (Section 17 ICA).
3. Negligence does not equal deceit.

cases.title: Daimler Co Ltd v Continental Tyre and Rubber Co (Great Britain) Ltd
cases.facts:
A company (Continental Tyre) was incorporated in England. However, all its directors and all but one of its
shareholders were German. During WWI, the company sued another company (Daimler) to recover a debt.
Daimler argued that although 'Continental' was an English company on paper, it was actually an 'alien enemy'
because it was controlled by Germans.
cases.issues:
1. Can the 'Corporate Veil' be lifted in contracts to determine the 'enemy' status of a party during war?
2. Is a contract with a company controlled by enemies void under Section 56 (Unlawful)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Daimler argued that looking at the 'nationality' of the company was a sham. The money would go to Germany
and help the war effort against England.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Continental argued that a company is a 'distinct legal person' from its shareholders. Since it was registered in
London, it was a 'loyal' English entity.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The House of Lords ruled in favor of Daimler, lifting the corporate veil.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that during wartime, the court must look at the 'economic reality'. A company is just a shell. If
the 'brain and heart' of the company (the directors and controllers) are based in an enemy country, the company
acquires 'enemy character'. Contracts with such entities become unlawful and are frustrated under the principle
of 'Trading with the Enemy'. The corporate veil was lifted to protect national security.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Lifting the Corporate Veil: Courts look behind the legal facade to the actual controllers in times of war
or fraud.
2. Enemy Character: Companies can take the nationality of their controllers during hostilities.
3. Contracts with enemies are void for being 'unlawful' (Section 56/23 ICA).

cases.title: M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore
cases.facts:
A father executed a deed in favor of his son, where the father promised to pay a debt to the Bank. The deed
stated that if the father didn't pay, the Bank could seize a specific property. The Bank was not a party to this
deed. When the father defaulted, the Bank sued the son to seize the property based on the father's promise in
the deed.
cases.issues:
1. Can a 'Stranger to a Contract' sue to enforce a promise made for its benefit in India?
2. What are the exceptions to the 'Doctrine of Privity'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The Bank argued that although they didn't sign the deed, they were the 'sole beneficiary' of the promise. Under
Indian law, they should be allowed to sue.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The son argued that the Bank was a 'stranger to the contract'. No one can sue on a contract unless they are a
party to it.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the son, upholding the Privity rule.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the Indian position on Privity. It held that while 'Privity of Consideration' is not required (a
stranger to consideration can sue), 'Privity of Contract' IS generally required. A person who is not a party to a
contract cannot sue on it, even if the contract is for their benefit. The Court listed narrow exceptions: (1) Trust,
(2) Family Settlement, (3) Acknowledgment of debt. Since the Bank didn't fit these, they couldn't enforce the
private deed between father and son.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Doctrine of Privity of Contract: Only parties to a contract can sue (General Rule in India).
2. Exceptions: Trust, marriage settlements, and family arrangements.
3. Beneficiaries have no automatic rights unless a 'Trust' is created.

cases.title: Arundel v. Bryant
cases.facts:
Bryant's horse was injured. Arundel, a passerby, voluntarily helped treat the horse and stayed with it for hours.
After the horse was better, Bryant thanked Arundel and promised to pay him £10 for his trouble. Later, Bryant
refused to pay.
cases.issues:
1. Can a promise be enforced if it is based on a 'past' voluntary act?
2. What is the status of 'Past Consideration' in English vs. Indian law?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Arundel argued that the promise was a valid recognition of his labor and should be binding as a contract.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Bryant argued that the work was already done before the promise was made. Therefore, there was no 'new'
exchange, and the promise was a mere gift.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of Bryant.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that 'Past Consideration is no consideration'. A promise made after the act is completed is not
part of a bargain. Since Arundel did the work voluntarily without any prior request, Bryant's later promise was
a nudum pactum (bare promise) and not enforceable. (Note: In India, Section 2(d) allows 'Past
Consideration' if it was done at the 'desire of the promisor', but voluntary acts are governed by Section 25(2)
which makes them enforceable as 'Past V oluntary Services').
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Past Consideration: Generally invalid in English Law.
2. Contracts require an exchange of promises or acts (Simultaneous or Future).
3. Moral obligation is not legal consideration.

cases.title: Harvey v. Facey
cases.facts: This case (revisited) defined the 'Offer' as a final expression of will.
cases.issues: 1. Is silence on 'willingness' fatal to an offer?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The buyer argued that by giving the price, the seller 'implicitly' said he was willing to sell.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The seller argued he was just a 'walking price list' and hadn't decided to sell yet.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled for the seller.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that an offer must be a 'final and definitive' expression of willingness to be bound. It is the 'last
word' in a negotiation. Since Facey only provided data (the price) and didn't provide consent (the will to sell),
he never made an offer. The buyer's 'acceptance' was therefore actually the first offer, which the seller rejected.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Offer vs. Information: Stating a fact is not making a promise.
2. The 'Mirror Image' requirement: You cannot accept what wasn't offered.
3. Intent must be manifest and unambiguous.
